cards.back: Fractional exponential increase in biomass or viable cell concentration per unit time.
Time required for an exponentially growing population to double, td=ln2/μ.
The volumetric gas-liquid mass-transfer coefficient, combining interfacial area and liquid-film transfer.
The rate at which a cell population consumes oxygen per cell or per culture volume.
Mechanical power input normalized by culture volume, often used as one scale-up criterion.
A smaller system designed to reproduce important gradients or stresses observed in a larger process.
A process variable whose variability can affect a critical quality attribute and therefore requires monitoring or control.
A measurable property that must remain within an appropriate limit or range to ensure product quality.
Reason across material inputs, gas paths, vessel connections, and sampling or harvest interfaces; the map does not specify a procedure.

cards.front: Log reduction in a simplified model
cards.back: For L = log₁₀(N₀/N), the modeled remainder is N = N₀ × 10⁻ᴸ; the arithmetic is not process validation or proof of sterility.
No detection applies to the tested sample and method; it does not establish absence throughout a vessel or batch.
OTR = kLa (C* − C) and OUR = q_O₂ × X; steady culture needs OTR ≥ OUR.
X_max = kLa (C* − C_crit) / q_O₂; supply is limited by kLa and by the driving force.
Higher kLa costs shear, foam and CO₂ stripping; higher C* raises oxidative-stress risk; both are design trade-offs.
Fitted kLa correlations hold inside the range of their data; measure kLa when geometry, scale or medium change.
dX/dt = μX, dG/dt = −q_G X, dP/dt = q_P X: specific rates times cell density.
ΔG = q_G X₀(e^(μt) − 1)/μ; multiply by 1000 to go from per mL to per L.
Each doubling consumes as much as all earlier ones combined.
dG/dt = D(G_in − G) − q_G X; D_min = q_G X/G_in, with cell retention.
μ = μ_max S/(K_s + S); half of μ_max at S = K_s, and a fraction f needs S = f K_s/(1 − f), so 90% needs 9 K_s.
X_max = X₀ + Y (S₀ − S_min); doubling S₀ roughly doubles the yield limit, but X_max is an upper bound if another factor stops growth first.
t = ln(X_max/X₀)/μ_max is a lower bound because of lag, deceleration and inhibition.
q_S = μ/Y_X/S, with the yield in cells per mmol; yields and maintenance uptake change with conditions.
μ = D; S_ss = D K_s/(μ_max − D); X_ss = Y (S₀ − S_ss). The residence time is 1/D.
D_crit = μ_max S₀/(K_s + S₀), slightly below μ_max; above it cells are removed faster than they grow and the culture washes out.
Output D X_ss peaks at D_opt = μ_max (1 − √(K_s/(K_s + S₀))), close to washout, so a margin is needed.
CSPR = perfusion rate/cell density, in pL/(cell·day); the minimum is uptake/(allowed consumption). Retention is never perfect.
P = N_p ρ N³ D⁵ (N in rev/s); P/V in W/m³; Re = ρND²/μ above about 10⁴ is turbulent; tip speed = πND.
Geometric similarity: P/V ∝ N³D², tip speed ∝ ND, Re ∝ ND², mixing time ∝ 1/N. Constant P/V gives N ∝ D^(−2/3).
Constant P/V: higher tip speed and longer mixing time. Constant tip speed: lower P/V. Constant speed: far higher P/V and tip speed.
Small vessels operated to reproduce the large vessel's mixing time and gradients expose cells to the large-scale environment before committing to it.
ε = (P/V)/ρ; η_K = (ν³/ε)^(1/4); stress at that scale τ = μ(ε/ν)^(1/2). A hundredfold rise in ε shrinks η_K by 3.16.
Cells much smaller than η_K see viscous shear; microcarriers and aggregates larger than η_K are exposed to eddies of their own size. Thresholds are empirical.
Dissipation is concentrated near the impeller; use the local value, with exposure time and frequency, not the average.

cards.front: Tip speed is a poor proxy
cards.back: In geometric similarity ε_max ∝ N³D² ∝ P/V, so constant P/V keeps the local eddy scale though the tip speed rises; bubbles damage cells separately.
OUR = qX; kLa_req = OUR/(C* − C_set). It grows as e^(μt) with the culture.
The vessel reaches kLa_max when e^(μt) = kLa_max/kLa_req0, so t = ln(kLa_max/kLa_req0)/μ.
Oxygen enrichment (higher C*), a lower setpoint or a higher kLa each extend the limit; each moves a hazard (oxidative stress, less margin, shear and foam).
The dissolved oxygen relaxes with 1/kLa; sensor lag matters when kLa times the probe response time is not small. Steady value C_ss = C* − OUR/kLa.
Effect = mean response at the high level − mean at the low level, over all runs; every run contributes to every effect.
AC = half the difference between the effect of A at high C and at low C; one-factor-at-a-time studies cannot see interactions.
Center points give s (with n − 1 degrees of freedom); SE(effect) = 2s/√N; curvature = center mean − factorial mean, with SE s√(1/N + 1/n_c).
2^k runs for k factors; a half fraction aliases effects (I = ABCD: A with BCD); randomize order, block by day or batch, and replicate independent cultures.
Count the independent runs and average the dissolved-oxygen readings at each time and speed; the run is the replicate.
ln(1 − C/C*) = −kLa t, with C in the same units as C*; use the time in hours for kLa per hour.
If kLa ∝ N^a and P/V ∝ N³, then kLa ∝ (P/V)^(a/3); a ≈ 1.5 means a square-root dependence on power per volume.
A cell-free test is a starting estimate; check kLa × τ_probe is small, and remember that cells, antifoam, medium and gas flow change kLa.
In an unsupplied region DO falls at the uptake: ΔC = OUR × t; time to the critical level = (C_bulk − C_crit)/OUR; Da = OUR t_mix/C_bulk.
Match the cell-level excursion (recirculation through an unsupplied region with the large-scale mixing time) at the same density, uptake and medium; keep everything else matched.
Cross environment (loop or control) with passage (early or late): the loop effect tests mixing, the passage effect in the control tests instability, and the interaction tests sensitivity.
The independent culture is the replicate; check n with the exact t power; sample at several positions and times, calibrate methods and count blind.

cards.front: What does an elemental balance close?
cards.back: For each element, total atoms in must equal total atoms out under the declared reaction.

cards.front: What is a C-mol of the stipulated biomass?
cards.back: One empirical biomass unit CH1.8O0.5N0.2 contains one carbon atom; its amount can be counted in C-mol.
Monod relates specific growth rate to substrate level; stoichiometry specifies an assumed atom allocation and yield.

cards.front: Does a closed synthetic balance validate a process?
cards.back: No. It checks the stipulated equation, not a pathway, real biomass formula, measured yield, or operating culture.
With feed and no outflow, dX/dt = (μ − D)X where D = F/V: added volume dilutes cells, but none are removed.
To hold substrate at S: F(S_F − S) = q_S N, so with exponential growth F(t) = q_S N₀e^(μt)/(S_F − S).
Cumulative feed q_S N₀(e^(μt) − 1)/(μ(S_F − S)) ends the run at the working volume, unless oxygen or by-products limit first.
Both have a D term, but in fed-batch it reflects volume growth: no washout, and product stays in the vessel.
With D = C* − C and OUR(t) = OUR₀ e^(μt), D′ + kD = OUR₀ e^(μt), D(0) = 0, so D(t) = OUR₀/(k + μ) × (e^(μt) − e^(−kt)).
Demand equals k(C* − Ccrit) before the dissolved oxygen actually reaches Ccrit, because oxygen already in the liquid is drawn down gradually.
At a dissolved-oxygen threshold Ccrit, the most oxygen transfer can supply is k(C* − Ccrit); compare it with the current uptake rate.

cards.front: How does cell retention change a constant-volume viable balance?
cards.back: Use the declared bleed/leakage loss coefficient separately from hydraulic substrate replacement; gross production must replace both viable export and death.

cards.front: Can a steady viable concentration hide ongoing death and replacement?
cards.back: Yes. Gross production, viable export and death can all be positive while their net balance is zero.

cards.front: Why define the numerator of a yield ratio?
cards.back: Exported viable biomass, gross production and a growth-associated coefficient refer to different boundaries and can differ when death, retention and maintenance are present.

cards.front: How do model-domain and discretization failures differ?
cards.back: A boundary derivative pointing outside the admissible domain is an equation-level issue; a negative numerical update despite an invariant exact model is a method/step issue.

cards.front: Why can an oxygen probe show a delayed rise while liquid transfer starts immediately?
cards.back: The probe is a separate dynamic state. Its initial slope can be zero although the liquid derivative is nonzero.

cards.front: How does structural nonidentifiability differ from noisy fitting?
cards.back: Distinct parameter assignments can give exactly the same ideal observations at every time; reducing noise or adding those same observations does not resolve the symmetry.

cards.front: How should a near-coincident exponential formula be verified?
cards.back: Check its analytic equal-rate limit and an independent ODE integration; cancellation in the direct expression is a numerical evaluation issue.

cards.front: What can a steady oxygen plateau identify in this model?
cards.back: With a known equilibrium concentration it constrains uptake divided by transfer; separate parameter values and transient behavior require more information.

cards.front: Why must internal exchange be written as an amount rate first?
cards.back: The same exchange amount enters one zone and leaves the other; dividing by each zone’s own volume then gives concentration derivatives that can differ.

cards.front: What does a closed total balance fail to establish by itself?
cards.back: It does not determine local exposure or validate a uniform driving-force approximation; local equations and observations carry additional information.

cards.front: When can better exchange solve a local deficit?
cards.back: Only when sufficient total supply keeps the supplied zone above the requested level; finite exchange cannot replace missing external capacity.

cards.front: What should a local-exposure study report beyond a bulk curve?
cards.back: Zone balances, weighted-total closure, admissibility, observation mapping and the assumptions held fixed in each controlled comparison.

cards.front: What belongs in a retained-state report?
cards.back: An outlet diagram, original equations, admissible steady branch, production/export/death and substrate ledgers, yield definitions and model-domain/transient evidence.

cards.front: Why retain separate viable and substrate ledgers?
cards.back: They have different state and amount bases. A matching viable net rate does not automatically close substrate, dead-material or elemental inventories.

cards.front: How can an accurate-looking fit estimate the wrong process coefficient?
cards.back: The observation can have its own dynamics and structural ambiguities; fit residuals do not validate the assumed mapping from process state to measured output.

cards.front: Why label separate model variants in an observation report?
cards.back: Equal-rate evaluation, rate assignment and constant uptake change different assumptions; their numerical results cannot be interchanged without re-solving the declared model.

cards.front: What distinguishes a spatial balance report from a single bulk fit?
cards.back: Separate zone volumes, local driving forces, equal/opposite exchange amount rates, local thresholds and a weighted-total residual are all retained.

cards.front: Why distinguish an internal mixing limit from external capacity?
cards.back: Redistribution can reduce local gaps, but it cannot supply oxygen that is missing from the external amount balance.

cards.front: What should a factorial endpoint report establish before interpreting effects?
cards.back: Schema and run identities, factor coding, cell means, the analysis unit and what the table’s synthetic construction does and does not support.

cards.front: Why can an averaged factor effect be misleading with interaction?
cards.back: The simple effect depends on the other factor level and can reverse sign. Endpoint patterns alone also do not identify the underlying physical mechanism.
